study.title: Beyond Antibunching: Photon Correlation Analysis Reveals Blinking Origin

cover.headline: **Different ways of measuring quantum light sources** can make identical devices look better or worse on paper

slides.title: If researchers keep using different methods, we can't tell which quantum light source is actually best.
slides.body:
Teams around the world are competing to build sources for quantum computers and secure messages. But they measure quality in different ways.

This paper shows the choice of method changes the reported quality for the same device.

slides.title: The team tested five methods now used in published papers to measure the same blinking quantum dot.
slides.body:
One method matched the true no-blinking result closely. Another gave results that were far off the mark.

The researchers then used their model to identify the blinking pattern in a quantum dot inside a circular Bragg grating cavity.

slides.title: The team took a quantum dot that doesn't blink and added blinking in two controlled ways.
slides.body:
They masked recorded data after the fact and gated laser pulses to copy a blinking system. Then they ran the data through each method.

Fitting the long-time pattern with the correct blinking model worked best. Poisson level adjustment performed worst.

caveats: This is a preprint. No independent expert has checked the work yet, because it hasn't been peer reviewed.
The experiment used quantum dots in a lab setup. Real-world quantum devices may behave differently under operating conditions.

source.abstract: A variety of quantum emitters compete in the quest for the best single-photon source for photonic quantum technologies. Consequently, only a consistent approach to analyze the second-order auto correlation function allows comparison of the multi-photon contribution ($g^{(2)}(0)$) of different sources. However, the community employs different and inconsistent methods for blinking sources, leading to incomparable benchmarks of source quality. Here, we use the emission of an inherently non-blinking quantum dot (QD) and apply artificial blinking through two different mechanisms: masking the recorded raw data in post-processing and emulation of a blinking system by gating the laser excitation pulses. We then compare the $g^{(2)}(0)$ values with the non-blinking result. For the analysis, we investigate five estimators of $g^{(2)}(0)$ actively used in the literature. While fitting the envelope of the correlations on long-time scales with the correct blinking model is the best choice, normalizing to the Poisson level gives by far the worst proximity. Furthermore, we test our predictive model to identify the underlying blinking mechanism of a QD in a circular Bragg grating cavity.
